opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think about it a lot. For me, the ChatGPT moment wasn't really about a benchmark number. It was the moment when ordinary people, not researchers, could interact with the system and feel that it just *works* across a huge range of things they cared about. You didn't need to be an expert, you didn't need to set anything up. You typed something, and it was useful.

So for Physical AI, I'd be convinced when we see something analogous in the physical world. A general-purpose robot, or a physical agent, that you can bring into a new environment it has never seen, a messy kitchen, a cluttered warehouse, someone's living room, and you give it a fairly open-ended instruction in natural language, and it completes the task reliably. Not one carefully engineered demo, but many different tasks, in many different places, without retraining or a team of engineers tuning it for weeks.

There are a few signals I'd look for. First, generalization: the same model handling different embodiments and different tasks, the way one language model handles writing, coding, and translation. Second, reliability: in the physical world a 90% success rate isn't good enough, because failures break things or hurt people. When we're in the high nineties on everyday tasks, that's a real shift. Third, the scaling story: in language, we saw that more data and more compute predictably gave better models. For Physical AI, the bottleneck has always been data. If world models and simulation, generating physically plausible synthetic experience, start giving us that same predictable scaling, I think that's the foundation for the moment.

And maybe the simplest test: when people outside our field start using these systems not because they're impressive, but because they're genuinely helpful in their daily lives or work. That's when you know it has arrived.

Honestly, I don't think we're there yet. But I think the pieces are coming together faster than many people expect. A few years ago, generating a coherent, physically consistent video of the world seemed very far away, and now it's becoming practical. So I'm optimistic, but I also think it'll be more gradual than ChatGPT was, because the physical world is just much less forgiving than text.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think about it a lot. For ChatGPT, the moment came when a general system could handle a task it was never explicitly trained on, and ordinary people could feel that in a few minutes of use. So for physical AI, I would want to see the same thing in the physical world.

Concretely, I would want to see a robot walk into a home or a factory it has never seen before, be given an instruction in plain language, and just do the job. Not a demo on a carefully arranged table, but a new environment, new objects, new lighting, and the robot adapts. And when it fails, it recovers rather than freezing. That is the generalization piece.

The second thing I would look for is the economics. ChatGPT mattered because the cost of getting a useful answer dropped close to zero. For physical AI, the equivalent is the cost of teaching a new task. Today, if you want a robot to do something new, you often need weeks of data collection and engineering. When that becomes a few hours, or a few demonstrations, or even just a text description, that is when deployment compounds.

And the third signal is the data flywheel. Language models had the whole internet. Robots do not have that, which is why we have been investing so much in simulation and world models. When robots in the field start generating data that improves the next model, and that model gets deployed back into more robots, you have a loop that is very hard to stop. When I see that loop actually turning, with real customers, not just research labs, I would say the moment has arrived.

My honest view is that we are not there yet. But the gap is closing faster than most people expect, because the same scaling recipe that worked for language appears to be working for physical understanding too.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key would be generalization. Imagine you bring a robot into a home it has never seen, and you ask it to help clean up after dinner. It has to understand what you mean, recognize unfamiliar objects, figure out how to handle them, and recover when something goes wrong—all without an engineer programming that particular kitchen.

One successful demonstration wouldn’t convince me. I would want to see that capability work reliably across many homes and many tasks, at a cost that makes it useful to people.

And then there’s the interaction: can an ordinary person teach it something new simply by talking to it or showing it? When people can use a robot to solve problems its developers didn’t explicitly anticipate, I think we’re very close to that ChatGPT moment for physical AI.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the convincing signal would be generalization. You give a robot a task it has never been explicitly trained to do, in an environment it has never seen, and it can understand your instruction and complete the task reliably. And when something goes wrong, it can recognize that and recover.

A beautiful demo is exciting, but I would want to see that capability work across many tasks, many environments, and many users. If an ordinary person can ask a robot for help without needing an engineer standing next to it, and the robot consistently does something useful, that would feel like Physical AI’s ChatGPT moment.
